title: CMake: Hardening compiler options
description:
Hardened compiler option should give us a more secure application against potential attacks and/or misbehavior

This is according to Best Practice from Open SSF

https://best.openssf.org/Compiler-Hardening-Guides/Compiler-Options-Hardening-Guide-for-C-and-C++

> For me the code becomes more readable doing that.

In that case that appears to be the only place it's used. If there are any other cases where the same format string is used repeatedly if might be more readable to have a const literal, but it should be `const`.

Changing to `static const char` (or move the text directly) solved that problem, then there are ex

```
epan/dissectors/packet-afp.c: In function ‘decode_name_label’:
epan/dissectors/packet-afp.c:1971:5: error: format not a string literal, argument types not checked [-Werror=format-nonliteral]
     ett_afp_path_name, NULL, label, name);
     ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

```
epan/dissectors/packet-asterix.c: In function ‘asterix_build_subtree’:
epan/dissectors/packet-asterix.c:59097:29: error: format not a string literal, argument types not checked [-Werror=format-nonliteral]
                             proto_tree_add_double_format_value (parent, *field->part[i]->hf, tvb, offset_in_tvb, length_in_tvb, value * scaling_factor, field->part[i]->format_string, value * scaling_factor);
                             ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

Both are tricky.. and many more like that

With the `asterix` examples:

* It's all code generated code.
* The code generated code produces `static const FieldPart` which are static initialized.
* `field->part[i]->format_string` is a `const char *`.
* The format string in practice seems to always be NULL, so maybe it's for future use.

So at least in that case that seems to be not a problem, possibly too many layers of indirection for the compiler to deduce that it's fine.

In `afp` ~~`name`~~ `label` is in fact always a string literal as passed to `decode_name_label`, so there's no problem in practice. I think there are some ways in other languages, like C++ with `consteval` and a wrapper, to guarantee that a function parameter is always a string literal (and not just that the function promises not to change it.)

All the labels passed in in `afp` are something like `"Source path: %s"`, so the function could be rewritten to just take in the `Source path:` part, and have its own literal format string like `"%-13s %s"` or some such.
(or "%*s %s" and pass in the width.)

Note that in general we check for any completely missing compiler flag, so there's no reason to do any checks unless the compiler flag exists in an earlier version of a compiler but is buggy so we don't want to use it.

Which apparently includes `_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` on some versions of gcc, where `test_compiler_flag` will report success but actually compiling will yield a warning that on that version (11.x), `FORTIFY_SOURCE=n` for `n > 2` is the same as for `2`.

`FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` has performance impacts and intentionally crash the program at runtime if it detects a possible issue (which in some cases may be a false positive.) We might not want to enable it for the Release build type and we ought to do some profiling and performance testing before having a release with it enabled.

Ubuntu builds with `FORTIFY_SOURCE=2` as default, and according to RedHat `FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` performance lost should be trival in practice.

https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2023/02/06/how-improve-application-security-using-fortifysource3
Correction, Ubuntu does `FORTIFY_SOURCE=3`  https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/gcc-13/+bug/2012440

mentioned in merge request !17264

The order of `-U` vs `-D` is critical. The purpose of `-U_FORTIFY_SOURCE` in the guidelines is to avoid conflicting with any default set by the compiler from e.g. distribution patches, then to _later_ set `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` to choose level 3. This is not particularly great and it would be better to use a macro like [AX_ADD_FORTIFY_SOURCE](https://www.gnu.org/software/autoconf-archive/ax_add_fortify_source.html), but it is what it is for now.

In any case, that pattern is not what you're implementing here. You're setting `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` (which may clash with e.g. a default of 2 in the compiler) and then unsetting both that _and_ any default with `-U_FORTIFY_SOURCE`, leaving no protection at all.

TL;DR: `-U_FORTIFY_SOURCE` must go first.
I've filed https://github.com/ossf/wg-best-practices-os-developers/issues/658 and https://github.com/ossf/wg-best-practices-os-developers/issues/659 to make this clearer.

commits_data.title: CMake: Hardening compiler options
commits_data.message:
CMake: Hardening compiler options

Hardened compiler option should give us a more secure application
against potential attacks and/or misbehavior

This is according to Best Practice from Open SSF
https://best.openssf.org/Compiler-Hardening-Guides/Compiler-Options-Hardening-Guide-for-C-and-C++
